PART THREE
Money & Work
CHAPTER 20
When You Worry About
Money
You know the price of things you used to put in the cart without
thinking. Before agreeing to a meal with friends, you work out
what it will cost. A bill can still trouble you after you have paid
it, because another one will come next month.
Sometimes the worry has a clear cause: less income, a necessary
expense, someone depending on you. Sometimes there is
enough for now, but you cannot trust that it will last. From the
outside, those situations can look much the same. Only you may
know how much calculation an ordinary day involves.
Jesus spoke directly about food and clothing. In Matthew
6:25–34, He places these needs within the Father's care. He
knows that people need to eat. His teaching gives us somewhere
to bring that concern when the arithmetic alone cannot settle it.
Asking for enough
Earlier in the same chapter, Jesus teaches His disciples to pray:
Give us this day our daily bread.
Matthew 6:11, Berean Standard Bible

99
Bread belongs in a prayer. So does the rent, or the money needed
to get to work. Some people find it easier to pray about becoming
more patient than to ask for help buying groceries. Perhaps a
material need seems too ordinary, or admitting it feels
uncomfortable. Jesus includes the need for food in the words He
gives His followers.
Notice the word "us." The prayer includes other people. When
someone lacks enough, the community praying these words has
reason to pay attention. Receiving practical help can belong to
the life of faith, alongside offering it.
There is also a limit in "this day." You may need to plan months
ahead, especially if others rely on you. But a plan cannot give
you advance possession of every resource you will ever need.
Prayer can attend to what is necessary now while the longer
questions remain open.
Food for the wilderness
Exodus 16
After leaving Egypt, the Israelites faced hunger in the
wilderness. God gave them manna to gather for food. They were
told how much to gather and, on ordinary days, not to keep it
until morning. Some kept it anyway, and it spoiled.
The instructions changed for the Sabbath, the day set apart for
rest. On the sixth day they gathered twice as much, and that
portion kept for the next day. The account includes both daily
dependence and provision made ahead for a specific need.
The people were learning to follow God's instructions in the
wilderness. The provision for the Sabbath helps us avoid
reading the story as a rule against saving for a future need. God
cared for people who had no harvest of their own to gather.
They still went out for the food. They measured it and brought it
home. Depending on God involved ordinary work as well as
receiving something they could not produce for themselves.

100
When trusting feels difficult
Habakkuk 3:17–18 imagines the loss of almost everything on
which an agricultural community depends: fruit, crops, sheep,
cattle. The prophet speaks of rejoicing in God even under those
conditions. The passage gives full attention to the possibility of
loss before expressing trust.
You might read it and find that you cannot yet say the same
words with confidence. Begin with the part you can name
honestly. "I am afraid there will not be enough." Or, "I do not
know how to provide for the people I love." A prayer can include
the question of how to trust while the need is still pressing.
In Matthew 6:26, Jesus asks His listeners to consider the birds
and then speaks of their own value to the Father. A small bank
balance can make a person feel overlooked, especially in a
setting where money brings influence and choice. Jesus' words
locate your value in the Father's regard for you.
Even without knowing how an expense will be met, you can ask
for His help. Your financial position does not put you beneath
His notice.
The people through whom care arrives
Paul writes about God's provision near the end of a letter
thanking people for their help:
And my God will supply all your needs according to His
glorious riches in Christ Jesus.
Philippians 4:19, Berean Standard Bible
The Philippians had shared in his trouble and sent gifts for his
needs. Their concern had taken a practical form.
Read the promise alongside that relationship. God's care need
not arrive as an unexplained change in your account. It may
involve someone sharing food, helping you understand a
problem, or making room for you to receive assistance. Paul

101
could speak about learning contentment and still thank people
for giving him what he needed.
Hebrews 13:5 connects contentment with God's promise to
remain with His people. Contentment can include appreciating
what is available today while asking for what is missing. A
family without enough food needs food; a call to trust God
should help us hear that need.
Put the immediate concern into words
Name the need that concerns you most this month. Is an
expense already beyond what you can cover, or are you afraid of
a possible change further ahead? The difference can help you
identify what needs action now and what you cannot yet settle.
Look at enough of the figures to understand that immediate
question. If there is a shortfall that cutting back will not solve,
acknowledge it. Asking for help with a specific need gives
someone a clearer way to respond than trying to carry every
possible future expense at once.
Then choose the next conversation the situation calls for. That
might be with someone in your household, a person who can
help you find local assistance, or a reputable credit counselor if
debt is involved. You can pray before that conversation,
including about the embarrassment or fear that makes it hard to
begin.
If someone you care about is worried about money
An invitation can be costly even when it sounds casual. Make
room for inexpensive ways to spend time together, without
requiring the person to explain why they prefer them.
If they tell you about financial pressure, ask what would help.
They might welcome a meal or company while making a
difficult call. Advice about spending can wait until you
understand what they are facing and whether they want advice.

102
Treat the details they share with care, and avoid turning their
need into a story you tell others.
A prayer
Father, You know what this month requires. I am afraid of what
may happen if there is not enough. Help me look clearly at the needs
in front of me and speak honestly with the people who can help.
Provide for my household. Teach me to receive care without hiding,
and to notice others whose needs I can share. In Jesus' name, amen.
Pause and reflect
What do you need to ask God for today, in plain and specific
words?
Who could help you understand the practical concern that
occupies most of your thoughts?
For further reading: Exodus 16; Habakkuk 3:17–19; Matthew 6:9–13, 19–34; Philippians
4:10–20; Hebrews 13:5–6; 1 Peter 5:7.
